source_text:
Ἢ γὰρ οὐχὶ ταῦτα, δογμάτων τε τὰ μαχόμενα καὶ ἐναντιούμενα ἀλλήλοις, φιλοσόφων τε τὰς στάσεις εἰσήγαγεν, ἄλλων τοῖς ἄλλων ἐνισταμένων δόγμασι, καὶ ἄλλων ἄλλα κρατούντων, ἄλλων τε ἄλλοις προστιθεμένων· καὶ φιλοσοφεῖν μὲν ἁπάντων βουλομένων καὶ ἐπαγγελλομένων ἐξ οὗ γε προὐτράπησαν τὸ πρῶτον, καὶ φασκόντων ἐθέλειν οὐχ ἧττον ὅτε γεγόνασιν ἐν τοῖς λόγοις, ἢ ὡς αὐτῶν ἤρχοντο, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ πλείονα τὸν ἔρωτα νῦν ἔχειν τῆς φιλοσοφίας, ὅτε αὐτῆς καὶ γεύσασθαι (ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις) ὑπῆρξε καὶ προσδιατρίψαι τοῖς λόγοις, ἤπερ ὅτε πρῶτον ἀπείρως ἔχοντες εἶθ' ὑπὸ ὁρμῆς τινος φιλοσοφεῖν ἐπήρθησαν· λεγόντων μὲν ταῦτα, οὐκέτι δ' ὑπακουσάντων λόγοις, οὐδέν ἐστι τῶν ἑτεροδόξων. οὔτ' οὖν εἷς τις τῶν παλαιῶν προὐτρέψατό τινα τῶν νεωτέρων ἢ τῶν τοῦ Περιπάτου πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐπιστρέφειν, καὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ φιλοσοφίαν φιλοσοφεῖν, οὔτε ἀνάπαλιν, καὶ ὅλως οὐδεὶς οὐδένα. οὐ γὰρ ἂν ῥᾳδίως μεταπεισθείη τις προσθέσθαι, τῶν αὐτοῦ μετατιθέμενος, ἑτέροις· καὶ ταῦτα τούτοις ἴσως, οἷς εἴπερ ἐπείσθη πρὶν φιλοσοφήσει προσελθεῖν, τὸ πρῶτον ἂν καὶ ἠγάπα, καὶ ἐπείσθη ῥᾳδίως· οἷα δὴ μὴ προκατειλημμένης τῆς ψυχῆς μηδέπω λόγοις, προσανείχετο ἂν καὶ ἠγάπα, ὁμοίως ἐναντιούμενος δι' ἐκεῖνα τούτοις, ἃ νῦν ἔχει.

Τοιαῦτα ἡμῶν οἱ καλοὶ καὶ λογιώτατοι καὶ ἐξεταστικώτατοι Ἕλληνες πεφιλοσοφήκασιν, οἷς προσέτυχεν ἕκαστος ἐξ ἀρχῆς, ἐλαθεὶς ὑπό τινος ὁρμῆς, ταῦτα μόνα λέγων εἶναι ἀληθῆ, τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ πάντα τῶν ἄλλων φιλοσόφων ἀπάτην καὶ λῆρον· λόγῳ μὲν οὐδὲν μᾶλλον αὐτὸς τὰ αὐτοῦ κρατύνων, ἢ τῶν ἄλλων ἕκαστοι προΐστανται τῶν ἰδίων, τοῦ μὴ χρῆναι μετατίθεσθαι καὶ μεταβουλεύεσθαι ἀνάγκῃ ἢ πειθοῖ, οὐκ ἄλλην τινά, εἰ δεῖ τ' ἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν, ἔχων, ἢ τὴν πρὸς τῆς φιλοσοφίας ἐπὶ τάδε τὰ δόγματα ἄλογον ὁρμήν, καὶ κρίσιν ὧν οἴεται ἀληθῶν (μὴ παράδοξον εἰπεῖν ᾖ) οὐκ ἄλλην ἢ τὴν ἄκριτον τύχην· ταῦθ' ἕκαστος φιλῶν, οἷς προσέτυχε τὸ πρῶτον, ὑφ' ὧν οἱονεὶ δεδεμένος, οὐκέθ' οἷός τε προσέχειν ἑτέροις· εἰ μέν τι καὶ λέγειν ἔχοι σὺν ἀποδείξει ἀληθείας τῶν αὐτοῦ περὶ πάντων, καὶ ὡς ψευδῆ εἴη τὰ τῶν ἐναντίων, βεβοηθημένος καὶ τῷ λόγῳ· ἐπεὶ καὶ ἀβοήθητος, ἑαυτὸν χαρισάμενος καὶ ἐκδεχόμενος εἰκῇ, ὥσπερ ἕρμαιον, τοῖς προκαταλαβοῦσιν αὐτὸν λόγοις· οἳ δ' ἔν τε τοῖς ἄλλοις ἔσφηλαν τοὺς ἔχοντας, καὶ δὴ καὶ τοῦ πάντων μεγίστου καὶ ἀναγκαιοτάτου, τῆς περὶ τὸ θεῖον γνώσεως καὶ εὐσεβείας. καὶ μένουσιν ὅμως ἐν αὐτοῖς δεδεμένοι τρόπον τινά, καὶ οὐκέτ' ἂν αὐτοὺς οὐδεὶς ῥύσαιτο ῥᾳδίως, ὥσπερ ἐκ τενάγους ἐν πεδίῳ πλατυτάτῳ δυσδιαβάτῳ, οὐκέτι ἐῶντος τοὺς ἐμπεσόντας ἅπαξ οὔτε παλινδρομήσαντας οὔτε καὶ περαιωσαμένους διασώζεσθαι, ἐν αὐτοῖς δὲ αὐτοὺς κατέχοντας μέχρι τελευτῆς· ἢ ὥσπερ ἐξ ὕλης βαθείας καὶ δασείας καὶ ὑψηλῆς, εἰς ἣν εἰσῆλθε μέν τις ὁδοιπόρος, ὡς δὴ καὶ ἐξορμήσων ἴσως, καὶ ἐν καθαρῷ πάλιν αὐτὸν καταστήσων τῷ ἕρκει, ὑπὸ δὲ μήκους καὶ δασύτητος οὐχ οἷός τε γίνεται, πάμπολλα στρεφόμενος ἐν αὐτῷ, ὁδούς τέ τινας ἔνδον εὑρίσκων συνεχεῖς, ποικίλα ὁδοιπορεῖ, ὡς δὴ διά τινος αὐτῶν ἐξορμήσων τάχα· αἱ δ' ἐπὶ τὰ ἔνδον ἄγουσι μόνον, ἔξοδον δὲ οὐδαμῶς, αὐτῆς τε τῆς ὕλης μόνης ὁδοί τινες οὖσαι. τέλος δὲ ὁ ὁδοιπόρος ἀποκαμὼν καὶ ἀπαγορεύσας, ὡς δὴ πάντων ὕλης γενομένων, καὶ οὐκέτι οὐδενὸς ὄντος ἐπὶ γῆς οἰκητηρίου, ἐκεῖ μένειν ἐθέλει, τὴν ἑστίαν καταστησάμενος, καὶ εὐρυχωρίαν αὐτῷ, ὡς οἷόν τε, ἐν τῇ ὕλῃ ἐκποριζόμενος. καὶ ὥσπερ ἔκ τινος λαβυρίνθου, εἰς ὃν εἰσόδου φαινομένης μιᾶς, οὐδὲν ποικίλον ἐκ τῶν ἔξωθεν ὑποτοπήσας τις, εἰσελθὼν διὰ τῆς φαινομένης θύρας μιᾶς, εἶτα προχωρήσας ἄχρι τῶν ἐνδοτάτω, ποικίλον τε ἰδὼν τὸ θέαμα καὶ κατασκεύασμα πάνσοφον, πολύπορόν τε καὶ εἰσόδοις καὶ ἐξόδοις συνεχέσι σεσοφισμένον, ἐθέλων μέντοι καὶ ἐξιέναι, μηκέθ' οἷός τε εἴη, ἐναποληφθεὶς ἔνδον ὑπὸ σοφοῦ δοκοῦντος αὐτῷ κατασκευάσματος. οὐδεὶς δὲ οὔτε λαβύρινθος οὕτω δυσεξέλικτος καὶ ποικίλος, οὔτε ὕλη δασεῖα καὶ ποικίλη, οὔτε πεδίον οὕτως ἢ τέναγος, δεινὸν κρατῆσαι τοὺς ἐμπελάσαντας, ὡς λόγος, εἴ τις εἴη κατ' αὐτῶν τῶνδέ τινων φιλοσόφων.

Ἵνα δὴ οὖν μὴ ταὐτὸν τοῖς πολλοῖς πάθοιμεν, πρὸς μὲν ἕνα τινὰ οὐκ ἦγε τῶν φιλοσόφων λόγων, οὐδὲ κατ' αὐτοὺς ἀπιέναι ἠξίου, πρὸς δὲ πάντας ἦγεν, οὐδενὸς ἀπειράστους εἶναι θέλων δόγματος Ἑλληνικοῦ. καὶ αὐτὸς δὲ συνεισῄει προηγούμενος καὶ χειραγωγῶν ὥσπερ ἐν ὁδοιπορίᾳ, εἴ που καὶ ὑπαντήσαι τι σκολιὸν καὶ ὕπουλον καὶ σοφισματῶδες, οἷα δὴ τεχνίτης ἐκ τῆς ἐκ πολλοῦ τοῖς λόγοις συνδιατριβῆς οὐκ ἀήθης οὐδενὸς οὐδὲ ἄπειρος ὤν, μετέωρος αὐτός τε ἐν ἀσφαλεῖ μένοι, καὶ ἄλλοις ὀρέγων χεῖρα διασώζοιτο, ὥσπερ βαπτιζομένοις ἀνιμώμενος· πᾶν μὲν ὅ,τι χρήσιμον φιλοσόφων ἑκάστων καὶ ἀληθὲς ἦν, ἀναλέγων καὶ παρατιθέμενος ἡμῖν· ὅσα δὲ ψευδῆ, ἐκκρίνων, τά τε ἄλλα, καὶ μάλιστα ὅσα ἴδια πρὸς εὐσέβειαν ἦν ἀνθρώπων.
thought_title: Why the schools hold their followers captive
orientation: Gregory explains how the schools hold their followers captive, and how Origen kept his students free by sifting what was true in each.
pass_a_gloss: Or is it not these things that brought in both the fighting and mutually opposed of the doctrines and the factions of philosophers, some resisting the doctrines of others, some holding some things, some attaching themselves to others; and all wishing and professing to philosophize from when they were first turned toward it, and claiming to desire it no less when they have come into the arguments than as they were beginning them, but rather to have now even more love of philosophy, when it has befallen them to taste it (as one might say) and to spend time in the arguments, than when at first, being inexperienced, they were then lifted up by some impulse to philosophize; saying these things, but no longer having listened to arguments, nothing is of the other-minded [sense: they heed none of those who think otherwise]. Not then has any one of the old persuaded any of the newer or of those of the Peripatos to turn to him and philosophize his philosophy, nor the reverse, and in short no one anyone. For one would not easily be persuaded over to attach himself to others, changing away from his own; and that perhaps to those which, if he had been persuaded of them before coming to philosophizing, he would at first have loved and been persuaded easily; since the soul was not yet pre-occupied by arguments, he would have held to and loved them, opposing in like manner because of those these things which he now holds. Such things our fine and most learned and most examining Greeks have philosophized: whatever each happened on from the beginning, driven by some impulse, saying these alone are true, and all the rest of the other philosophers deceit and nonsense; by argument no more strengthening his own than each of the others champion their own; for not needing to change over and re-deliberate by necessity or persuasion, having no other (reason), if one must speak the truth, than the irrational impulse at the side of / toward philosophy upon these doctrines, and judgment of what he thinks true (let it not be paradoxical to say) no other than undiscerning chance; each loving these which he first happened on, by which as it were bound, no longer able to attend to others; if indeed he has something to say with demonstration of truth of his own about all things, and that the things of the opponents are false, being helped also by argument; but even unhelped, having given himself and receiving at random, like a windfall, the arguments which seized him first; which have tripped their holders both in other things and indeed made them fail of the greatest and most necessary of all, the knowledge and piety concerning the divine. And they remain nevertheless bound in them in a way, and no one would any longer easily rescue them, as from a marsh in a very broad plain hard to cross, no longer allowing those once fallen in to be saved either running back or crossing over, but holding them in them until the end; or as from a forest deep and dense and high, into which some traveler entered, as indeed perhaps intending to set out from it and set himself again in the clear by the fence/enclosure, but by its length and density he is not able, turning about very much in it, and finding some continuous paths inside, he travels variously, as if to get out by one of them; but they lead only inward, and to no exit at all, being some paths of the forest itself alone. Finally the traveler, worn out and giving up, as if all had become forest and there were no longer any dwelling on earth, wishes to stay there, setting up his hearth, and procuring for himself open space, as far as possible, in the forest. And as from some labyrinth, into which, one entrance appearing, someone suspecting nothing intricate from the outward things, entering through the one door that appears, then going forward to the innermost parts, and seeing the varied sight and all-wise construction, many-passaged and cunningly made with continuous entrances and exits, wishing indeed to go out, he might no longer be able, caught inside by a construction seeming wise to him. But there is no labyrinth so hard to unwind and intricate, nor forest dense and varied, nor plain thus or marsh, terrible at holding those who approach, as argument, if there should be any, according to some of these very philosophers. So that then we might not suffer the same as the many, he did not lead to some one of the philosophers' doctrines, nor think it right to go off after them, but led to all, wishing us to be untried in no Greek doctrine. And he himself went in with us, leading the way and leading by the hand as on a journey, if anywhere something crooked and festering beneath and sophistical should meet us, as a craftsman, from long familiarity with arguments being unaccustomed to nothing nor inexperienced, he himself might stay aloft in safety, and stretching a hand to others might save them, as drawing up for those sinking; gathering up and setting before us all that was useful and true of each of the philosophers; but whatever was false, sifting out, both the other things and especially whatever was proper to men regarding piety.

pass_b_english: Is it not this that has brought in the doctrines that fight and contradict one another, and the factions of the philosophers, some opposing the doctrines of others, some holding fast to one set of views and others attaching themselves to another? All of them, from the time they were first turned toward philosophy, want to practice it and profess that they do. They claim that they desire it no less now that they are deep in its arguments than when they were beginning them; rather, that they love philosophy even more now, when it has been granted them to taste it, so to speak, and to spend their time in its arguments, than when at first, knowing nothing of it, they were carried away by some impulse to philosophize. So they say; yet they will no longer listen to the arguments of anyone who thinks otherwise. So not one of the older philosophers ever persuaded any of the newer ones, or any of the Peripatetics, to turn to him and follow his philosophy, nor the other way round; in short, no one ever persuaded anyone. For no one would easily be won over to give up his own views and join others, and that perhaps the very views which, had he been persuaded of them before he came to philosophy, he would have loved from the first and accepted easily. Since his soul was not yet taken over by any arguments, he would have held to them and loved them, and for their sake would have opposed, in just the same way, the views he now holds.

Such is the philosophy of these fine Greeks of ours, most learned and most searching as they are. Whatever each one happened upon at the start, driven by some impulse, that alone he calls true, and all the views of the other philosophers he calls deceit and nonsense. He does not support his own views by argument any more than each of the others champions theirs; and for refusing to change his mind or think again, whether pressed by necessity or by persuasion, he has, if the truth must be told, no other ground than the unreasoning impulse that, as he came to philosophy, drew him to these doctrines, and no other judge of what he thinks true, if it is not too strange a thing to say, than undiscerning chance. Each loves the views he first happened upon, and, bound by them as it were, he can no longer give heed to any others. If he can say something to prove the truth of his views on every point, and to show that his opponents' views are false, then he has argument on his side as well; but even without that help he has surrendered himself to the arguments that took hold of him first, welcoming them at random like a lucky find. These arguments have tripped up those who hold them in other matters, and above all have made them miss the greatest and most necessary thing of all, the knowledge of the divine and reverence toward it. Yet they stay bound in them, in a way, and no one could easily rescue them any longer. It is like a marsh in a vast plain that is hard to cross: once people have fallen in, it no longer lets them save themselves either by turning back or by getting across, but holds them there until they die. Or it is like a deep, dense, towering forest. A traveler goes in, perhaps meaning to come out again and set himself once more in open ground within the fences, but because of its length and thickness he cannot. He turns this way and that many times inside it, and, finding paths within that run on and on, he wanders along them in every direction, thinking he may soon get out by one of them; but they only lead further in and never out, for they are paths of the forest alone. At last the traveler, worn out and giving up, as though the whole world had become forest and there were no longer any dwelling on earth, decides to stay there, sets up his hearth, and clears himself what space he can in the forest. Or it is like a labyrinth. Only one entrance shows, so a man suspects nothing intricate from what he sees outside; he goes in through the single door that appears and walks on to the innermost parts. There he sees an intricate sight, a construction of great cunning, full of passages and cleverly contrived with entrances and exits one after another; and when he wants to leave, he can no longer do so, shut in by a construction that had seemed so clever to him. Yet no labyrinth is so hard to escape and so intricate, no forest so dense and tangled, no plain or marsh so terrible at holding those who come near it, as an argument can be when it is the argument of some of these philosophers.

So that we should not suffer the same fate as most people, he did not lead us to any single one of the philosophers' doctrines, nor did he think it right for us to go off after them; he led us to them all, wanting us to leave no Greek doctrine untried. He himself went in with us, leading the way and taking us by the hand, as on a journey. If anything crooked, unsound beneath its surface, or full of sophistry should confront us, he, a master of the craft to whom, after his long familiarity with arguments, nothing was strange and nothing untried, would stay safely above it himself and, stretching out his hand to others, would bring them through, drawing them up like people who are sinking. He gathered and set before us everything that was useful and true in each of the philosophers, and he sifted out whatever was false, in other matters and above all in whatever, where piety was concerned, was merely human.
notes: Copy-text: 1622 Paris Greek column (printed pp. 70-72); paragraph breaks before Τοιαῦτα and Ἵνα δὴ οὖν follow Koetschau, as in the source row. Doubtful reading: the print has λόγοις, οὐδέν ἐστι τῶν ἑτεροδόξων, which does not construe cleanly and is the same letters as A's οὐδένεσι divided into two words; the other witnesses' οὐδένεσι / οὐδέσι point to 'to none of the other-minded', and the English follows that sense ('no longer listen to the arguments of anyone who thinks otherwise'). παλαιοί / νεώτεροι rendered 'older philosophers' / 'newer ones'; a reference to the Old and New Academy is possible but not stated, so left general. The print keeps καὶ ἐπείσθη ῥᾳδίως (bracketed by Koetschau as a gloss); translated ('accepted easily'). At πρὸς τῆς φιλοσοφίας the sense is uncertain (a marginal conjecture reads πρὸς τὴν φιλοσοφίαν); rendered 'the unreasoning impulse that, as he came to philosophy, drew him to these doctrines'. ἐν αὐτοῖς δὲ αὐτοὺς κατέχοντας (print; Koetschau ἐν αὐτῷ … κατέχοντος) is loose in grammar; rendered by its plain sense 'holds them there until they die'. τῷ ἕρκει ('the fence, enclosure') is taken as the fenced open land outside the forest. The closing clause ὡς λόγος, εἴ τις εἴη κατ' αὐτῶν τῶνδέ τινων φιλοσόφων is rendered 'as an argument can be when it is the argument of some of these philosophers'. ὅσα ἴδια πρὸς εὐσέβειαν ἦν ἀνθρώπων (literally 'whatever was proper to men regarding piety') is rendered 'whatever, where piety was concerned, was merely human' (ἴδια … ἀνθρώπων, men's own), which leads into the next section's 'in these matters'. βαπτιζομένοις ἀνιμώμενος ('drawing up the sinking') may recall Peter sinking (Matthew 14:30-31); too uncertain to cite. At the close, κατ' αὐτῶν stands in A as well (Bengel's margin καταντῶν), so the print reading is kept. τοῦ … ἀναγκαιοτάτου after ἔσφηλαν is a genitive of what they were made to miss ('made them miss the greatest … thing').
